In general, this paper employs a control-theoretic approach to analyze feedback channels, which has been inspired by, e.g., [6], [7], [19] (Bode integral), [7], [12]–[14], [20], [21] (stochastic control and/or Kalman filter), as well as [10], [11] (Youla parametrization), in a broad sense; see also [22] and the references therein. One difference from the previous works, however, is that in this paper we adopt a particular variant of the Kalman filter that can deal with the first-order AR noises without extending the state to be estimated in Kalman filtering systems, as introduced in [23], and generalize the approach to cope with any finite-order ARMA noises. Another difference is that we examine the algebraic Riccati equation associated with the Kalman filter in a “non-recursive” characterization recently developed in [24]. Accordingly, we establish the connection between this variant of the Kalman filter and a feedback channel with any finite-order ARMA noises, after carrying out a series of equivalent transformations. In light of this connection, we obtain explicit lower bounds on the feedback capacity for any finite-order ARMA noises, by designing the parameters of the plant in the Kalman filtering system in a structural way. In addition, this variant of the Kalman filter naturally provides explicit recursive coding schemes with clear structures to achieve the lower bounds.

The lower bounds presented in this paper are seen to be consistent with various existing (analytic or explicit) results in the literature. Specifically, our bounds are shown to be tight for the first-order ARMA noises [3] (see also [9]) and a special class of the second-order MA noises [4]. Meanwhile, our results are seen to reduce to the lower bounds for any finite-order AR noises of [19] (see also [18]). Particularly, in comparison to the explicit expression of feedback capacity for any finite-order ARMA noises derived in [9] (see Theorem 18 therein), 1) what we obtained are lower bounds; 2) our explicit expression admits a simpler form; 3) it is not yet fully clear what the relationship between the two is. (Note that the approach taken in [9] was not from the perspective of Kalman filters.) In general, our results shall complement those of [9] in the sense that examining the gap between the expressions of [9] and ours might likely either simplify the expression in [9] or point to structures of the plant parameters with tighter bounds in our approach; in either case, additional insights will be gained into the feedback capacity problem. On the other hand, the explicit recursive coding schemes developed in this paper also complement the existing ones in the literature (see, e.g., [3], [19]).

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II provides technical preliminaries. Section III presents the main results. Concluding remarks are given in Section IV.

I. PRELIMINARIES

In this paper, we consider real-valued continuous random variables and discrete-time stochastic processes they compose. All random variables and stochastic processes are assumed to be zero-mean for simplicity and without loss of generality. We represent random variables using boldface letters. The logarithm is defined with base 2. A stochastic process $\{x_k\}$ is said to be asymptotically stationary if it is stationary as $k \to \infty$, and herein stationarity means strict stationarity [25]. Note in particular that, for simplicity and with abuse of notations, we utilize $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ to indicate that $x$ is a real-valued random variable and that $x$ is a real-valued $n$-dimensional random vector, respectively. Definitions and properties of the information-theoretic notions such as entropy rate $h_\infty(x)$ can be found in, e.g., [26].

A. Feedback Capacity

Consider an additive colored Gaussian noise channel with feedback given as
$y_k = x_k(m, y_{1,...,k-1}) + z_k, k = 1, 2, \ldots$
where $\{x_k\}, x_k \in \mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel input, $\{y_k\}, y_k \in \mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel output, $\{z_k\}, z_k \in \mathbb{R}$ denotes the additive noise that is assumed to be stationary colored Gaussian, and $m$ denotes the message. The feedback capacity $C_t$ of such a channel with power constraint $\overline{P}$ is defined as [2]
$C_t = \lim_{k \to \infty} \sup_{x_{1,...,k}} \frac{I(m; y_{1,...,k})}{k}$
$= \lim_{k \to \infty} \sup_{x_{1,...,k}} \frac{h(y_{1,...,k}) - h(z_{1,...,k})}{k}$, (1)
where the supremum is taken over all channel input $x_{1,...,k}$ that satisfy
$\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i=1}^{k} \mathbb{E}(x_i^2(m, y_{1,...,i-1})) \le \overline{P}$. (2)
Recently in [3], it was discovered that (1) is equal to
$C_t = \sup\{h_\infty(y) - h_\infty(z)\}, \quad (2)$
where the supremum is taken over all stationary channel input processes $\{x_k\}$ of the form
$x_k = \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} b_i z_{k-i}, b_i \in \mathbb{R}, \quad (3)$
while satisfying
$\mathbb{E}(x_k^2) \le \overline{P}$.
In fact, [3] provided a sequence of equivalent characterizations of the feedback capacity, whereas for the purpose of this paper, it suffices to adopt the characterization of (2) and (3) herein (see the proof of Theorem 3).

B. Lower Bounds on Feedback Capacity and Feedback Coding

We now proceed to obtain lower bounds on feedback capacity as well as the corresponding recursive coding schemes to achieve them, based upon the results and discussions provided in the previous subsection. We first propose a particular way to design $A$ and $C$. 

**Theorem 1:** Suppose that

\begin{equation}F^{-1}(z) - \gamma = \frac{1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}z^{-i}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{q} g_{j}z^{-j}} - \gamma,
\end{equation}
(25)

with a given $\gamma \in \mathbb{R}, \gamma \neq 0$, has at least $n \geq 1$ distinct nonminimum-phase zeros. Let

\begin{equation}A = T
\begin{pmatrix}
\lambda_{1} & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & \lambda_{2} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & \lambda_{n}
\end{pmatrix}
T^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n},
\end{equation}
(26)

where $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, \ldots, \lambda_{n}, \lambda_{1} \neq \lambda_{2} \neq \cdots \neq \lambda_{n}$, are picked among the nonminimum-phase zeros of (25). Note that conjugate zeros of (25), if there are any, should be picked in pairs in order to render $A$ a real matrix. Note also that herein $T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ can be any invertible matrix. In addition, choose a $C \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times n}$ that renders $(A, C)$ observable, e.g.,

\begin{equation}C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix} T^{-1},
\end{equation}
(27)

Then, in the system of (24) and Fig. 3, it holds for any $\ell = 1, \ldots, n$ that

\begin{equation} \left( \prod_{\ell = 1}^{n} \lambda_{\ell}^2 - 1 \right) \sigma_v^2 = \gamma^2 CP C^{\mathrm{T}} \\
= \left( \frac{1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}\lambda_{\ell}^{-i}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{q} g_{j}\lambda_{\ell}^{-j}} \right)^2 CP C^{\mathrm{T}}.
\end{equation}
(28)

**Proof:** Suppose that $A$ and $C$ are chosen as in (26) and (27), respectively. Clearly,

\begin{equation} \frac{1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}\lambda_{\ell}^{-i}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{q} g_{j}\lambda_{\ell}^{-j}} = \cdots = \frac{1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}\lambda_{n}^{-i}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{q} g_{j}\lambda_{n}^{-j}} = \gamma, \end{equation}
(29)

and it then follows from (19) that

\begin{equation}F^{-1}(A) = T
\begin{pmatrix}
1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}\lambda_{n}^{-i} & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & \cdots & 1 - \sum_{i=1}^{p} f_{i}\lambda_{n}^{-i} \\
\end{pmatrix}
T^{-1} = \gamma I.
\end{equation}

As such,

\begin{equation}\hat{C}P\hat{C}^{\mathrm{T}} = CF^{-1}(A) PF^{-1}(A) C^{\mathrm{T}} = \gamma^2 CP C^{\mathrm{T}}.
\end{equation}

1 & 1 & \ldots & 1 \\
\lambda_1 & \lambda_2 & \ldots & \lambda_n \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ldots & \vdots \\

=
\prod_{0 \leq i < j \leq n} (\lambda_j - \lambda_i),
\]

and \(\lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 \neq \cdots \neq \lambda_n\). Hence, (23) holds, which can then be rewritten as

\[\gamma^2 C P C^T = [ \begin{pmatrix} \prod_{\ell=1}^{n} \lambda_\ell^2 \end{pmatrix} - 1] \sigma_\xi^2,\]

since

\[\hat{C} P \hat{C}^T = \gamma^2 C P C^T.\]

Therefore, (28) follows by noting also (29).

Note in particular the fact that conjugate zeros of (25) are included in pairs in particular pairs.

There is an invariant for a shooting problem.

Note also that

\[
n \leq \max \{p, q\},
\]

since (25) has at most \(\max \{p, q\}\) zeros.

Meanwhile, we may obtain an equivalent form of the system given in (24) and Fig. 3.

Theorem 2: The system in Fig. 3 is equivalent to that in Fig. 4, where \(K(z)\) is dynamic and is given as

\[
K(z) = F^{-1}(z) \hat{K} = \frac{1 - \sum_{i=1}^p f_i z^{-i}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^q g_j z^{-j}} \hat{K}.
\]

(32)

where \(\hat{K} = F(z)(A - uu^T) \hat{F}(z)\). Because \(\hat{K} = F(A) - uu^T\), the differential version of the control system in (32) is automatically derived: for the same \(u\) and \(k\), the power of \(K(z)\) is reduced by the same factor. The design problem can be solved in closed form.

Proposition: Duality. Suppose \(F(z) = \sum_{i=1}^p a_i z^{-i} \hat{F}(z)\), and \(\hat{K}\) is defined by (32). If \(K(z)\) is properly isolated, then there exists a unique \(\hat{K}\) such that \((K(z), K(z))\) forms a balanced pairing for \(\hat{C}\), with \(\hat{C}\) given by the diagonalized form (23). That is,

\[
\hat{C} = P^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^p a_i f_i z^{-i} \hat{F}(z).
\]

Notice that this "static-dynamic equivalence" transformation, where \(C F^{-1}(A)\) is static and \(F^{-1}(z)C\) is dynamic, is a critical step. Consequently, the system of Fig. 5 is equivalent to that of Fig. 6. Moreover, since all the sub-systems are linear, the system of Fig. 6 is equivalent to that of Fig. 7, which in turn equals to the one of Fig. 4; note that the formulation of Fig. 5 is a stable and minimal-phase, and thus there will be no issues caused by cancellations of unstable poles and nonminimum-phase zeros. Meanwhile, the closed-loop stability of the system given in (33) and Fig. 4 is the same as that of the system given by (24) and Fig. 3, since they are essentially the same feedback system.

Hence \(K(z)\) is found by solving the equation (29) that forms a balanced pair with \(K(z)\) and its Keras feed

Note in particular that in the system of (33) and Fig. 4, it holds that
\[
\mathbb{E} \left[ ( \mathbf{y}_k' )^2 \right] = \mathbb{E} \left[ (C \mathbf{x}_k )^2 \right] = \mathbb{E} \left[ ( C \mathbf{x}_k - C \mathbf{x}_k )^2 \right]
\]
\[
= C \left\{ \mathbb{E} \left[ ( \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k ) ( \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k )^T \right] \right\} C^T = CP C^T,

(34)

since the system is LTI and \( \{ \mathbf{x}_k - \mathbf{x}_k \} \) is stationary.
We next provide a key observation that enables relating the Kalman filtering system to the feedback capacity.
Observation 1: In the system of (33) and Fig. 4, or equivalently, in the system of Fig. 8, we may view
\[
\mathbf{e}_k' = - \mathbf{y}_k' + \mathbf{v}_k
\]
(35)

as a feedback channel [3, [6] with ARMA noise \( \{ \mathbf{v}_k \} \),
where \( \{ - \mathbf{y}_k' \} \) is the channel input while \( \{ \mathbf{e}_k' \} \) is the channel output. Moreover, as illustrated in Fig. 8,
\[
L(z) = C(zI - A)^{-1} K(z)
\]
(36)

may be viewed as the feedback coding scheme; cf. [6], or alternatively, [3] with
\[
B(z) = \frac{-L(z)}{1 + L(z)} = \frac{-C(zI - A)^{-1} K(z)}{1 + C(zI - A)^{-1} K(z)}
\]
(37)

Meanwhile, with the notations in (35), the feedback capacity is given by (cf. the definition in (2))
\[
C_f = \sup_{ \{ - \mathbf{y}_k' \} } [ h_\infty (\mathbf{e}') - h_\infty (\mathbf{v}) ],
\]
(38)

where the supremum is taken over all stationary channel input processes { \( y_k' \) } of the form
\[
- y_k' = \sum_{i=1}^\infty b_i \mathbf{v}_{k-i}, \quad b_i \in \mathbb{R},
\]
(39)

while satisfying
\[
\mathbb{E} \left[ ( - \mathbf{y}_k' )^2 \right] = \mathbb{E} \left[ (y_k')^2 \right] \leq \bar{P}.
\]
(40)

As such, if \( A \) and \( C \) are designed specifically as in Theorem 1, then (36) provides a class of sub-optimal feedback coding scheme as long as (40) is satisfied, and the corresponding
\[
h_\infty (\mathbf{e}') - h_\infty (\mathbf{v})
\]
(41)

is thus a lower bound of (38).
Proof: Note that herein we have used the fact that \( \{ - \mathbf{y}_k' \} \) is stationary and \( - \mathbf{y}_k' \) is a linear combination of the past \( \{ \mathbf{v}_k' \} \) up to time \( k - 1 \), i.e., (39) holds. To see this, note first that, according to Theorem 2, the system in (33) and Fig. 4 is stable (and LTI). In particular, the transfer function from \( \{ \mathbf{v}_k' \} \) to \( \{ - \mathbf{y}_k' \} \), given as
\[
\frac{-C(zI - A)^{-1} K(z)}{1 + C(zI - A)^{-1} K(z)}
\]
(42)

is stable (and LTI). Then, since \( \{ \mathbf{v}_k' \} \) is stationary, \( \{ - \mathbf{y}_k' \} \) is also stationary. On the other hand, it can be verified that (42) is strictly causal, since
\[
K(z) = F^{-1}(z) \hat{K} = \frac{1 - \sum_{j=1}^q f_j z^{-j}}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^q g_j z^{-j}}
\]
(43)

is causal. As a result, (39) holds.

Based upon Observation 1, the following lower bound of feedback capacity can be obtained.
Theorem 3: Given an \( n \geq 1 \), suppose that
\[
\left\{ \begin{array}{lcl}
1 - \sum_{i=1}^p f_i \lambda_i^{-1} & = & \zeta \left( 1 + \sum_{j=1}^q g_j \lambda_i^{-j} \right), \\
& & \vdots \\
1 - \sum_{i=1}^p f_i \lambda_i^{-1} & = & \zeta \left( 1 + \sum_{j=1}^q g_j \lambda_i^{-j} \right), \\
& & \zeta^2 \frac{\bar{P}}{\sigma_\zeta^2} = \prod_{\ell=1}^n \lambda_\ell^{2} - 1,
\end{array} \right.
\]
(44)

has at least one solution \( [\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n]^T \) that satisfies \( |\lambda_\ell| > 1, \ell = 1, \ldots, n \) while \( \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 \neq \cdots \neq \lambda_n \) and \( \prod_{\ell=1}^n \lambda_\ell \in \mathbb{R} \); note that herein \( \zeta \in \mathbb{R}, \zeta \neq 0 \), is an auxiliary parameter. Among all such solutions, denote the one that provides the largest \( \prod_{\ell=1}^n \lambda_\ell \) as \( [\bar{\lambda}_1, \ldots, \bar{\lambda}_n]^T \). Then, a lower bound of the feedback capacity with ARMA noise (11) and power constraint \( \bar{P} \) is given by
\[
\log \left| \prod_{\ell=1}^n \bar{\lambda}_\ell \right|.
\]
(45)

Proof: Note first it is supposed that (43) has at least one solution \( [\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n]^T \) that satisfies \( |\lambda_\ell| > 1, \ell = 1, \ldots, n \) while \( \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2 \neq \cdots \neq \lambda_n \), which implicates that \( \lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots, \lambda_n \) are in fact distinctive nonminimum-phase zeros of

In this section, we introduce the concept and methods associated with Tomography Computed Tomography (CT), which is a crucial imaging modality in medical diagnostics. CT utilizes X-rays and other ionizing radiation sources to capture multiple thin slices of the body, and then using mathematical algorithms to reconstruct these slices into a 3D image of the internal structure. There are multiple CT scanners, each with its own considerations and limitations. In this dissertation we focus on the Slice-Echo CT scanner of the Siemens Sensation CT64 system of 2018. For more information on CT and CT Image Analysis, please refer to Mihatovic’s work [46, 47, 48]. Tomography Computed Tomography (CT) is a technique used in medical imaging to create detailed images of the internal structures of the body. It works by passing X-rays through the body and measuring the amount of the X-rays that are attenuated by each slice of the object and x-ray attenuation depends only on the material density and atomic number. This parameter is called relative X-ray attenuation (x Ra) and it is described by: said by: $$R(x)  =  \sum_{j=1}^{n}w_j \beta_j(x)$$ wherein $w_j$ is the mass density of thing $j$, and $\beta_j(x)$ is a function of the value of $j$ along the line $x$. A CT scanner consists of X-rays source, an X-ray detector, collimators, and imaging software used for processing images. While imaging software is crucial for obtaining accurate images after CT, accumulation of noise can still be an issue. Hence, the image signal is so corrupted by noise. Hence, the most suitable process for further processing is filtering of the signal in the frequency domain as well as the spatial in a combination where low cutoff frequencies and high cut off frequencies are preferred. We apply function $C(x)$ after low-pass filtering, in order to set the cutoff frequencies. One may analogously implement the equation above for the filter $C(x)$. Since the correction error does not reach the noise limit for typical noise, we will get uniformly distributed values $ \bar{\varepsilon}$ with the mean value $m$, and standard deviation $s$. In order to restore these corrupted signal values $\varepsilon_{n-i}$ the correction has to be followed by applying logarithm to the signal value. As we believe the information content is more important than the actual value of signal, we also can use logarithmic values as the output signal of the system. We aim at compensating for errors in this logarithm and estimating a common value which has the following characteristics: - For a fixed amount of errors in the logarithm, the estimation of common value will be accurate. - As error increases, the estimation of common value becomes even more accurate. - Values are found that are closer to logarithm of un-corrupted input value than the exact logarithm. This approach can be expanded to other signals like Audio signals or the codes of radio and TV channels [50]. IV. CONCLUSION

In this paper, from the perspective of a variant of the Kalman filter, we have obtained explicit lower bounds on the feedback capacity of channels with any finite-order ARMA Gaussian noises, as well as the accompanying recursive coding schemes to achieve them. Potential future research problems include investigating the tightness of the lower bounds beyond the cases considered in this paper.

It is also worth mentioning that the results presented in this paper represent the relatively preliminary explorations under the current framework; particularly, we considered a very special class of the plant parameters \(A\) and \(C\) with a simple structure. For future research, it might be interesting to investigate further the structure of the plant parameters, to make use of the yet unexploited degrees of freedom therein, which may potentially lead to tighter bounds and gain additional insights into the feedback capacity problem.

For another possible future research direction, examining the gap between the expressions of [9] and ours might likely either simplify the expression in [9] or point to structures of the plant parameters with tighter bounds in our approach.
